title: Module 7 — service desk, SLAs, and incident management

spans.caption: A ticket flow from intake through priority, investigation, resolution, and user confirmation.

spans.text: A ticket is the traceable record of a support request. Typical stages are intake, categorization and priority, assignment, diagnosis, resolution, user confirmation, and closure. Record who and what is affected, symptoms, start time, error text, actions taken, and next update time. Never include a password, MFA code, or unnecessary personal data.

Priority combines impact and urgency using the organization’s matrix. A critical service outage affecting many users is generally higher priority than a minor request from one user. Establish the actual scope and any workaround, then apply the approved matrix. High priority requires prompt response and escalation but does not bypass safe change controls.

A Service Level Agreement (SLA) may define response and resolution targets, service hours, and responsibilities; a response target is not the same as a full-resolution time. Priority, service calendar, and pause rules affect the SLA clock. If a target is at risk, update the user proactively and escalate to the owner. Do not promise an unverified completion time; give a clear next-update time.

In ITIL 4, an incident is an unplanned service interruption or reduction in quality; a service request is a standard user request. Incident management aims to restore service quickly and limit impact; root-cause analysis is a separate Problem Management activity. Work through logging, prioritization, initial diagnosis, escalation, resolution, and closure. A workaround may help users without removing the underlying cause.

Be clear, empathetic, and concise: acknowledge impact, explain verified facts and the next step, then check understanding. Avoid unexplained jargon and state which service and users are affected. Be honest about delays and uncertainty; do not blame. Record the preferred contact channel, suitable time, and commitments in the ticket.

Begin with safe, repeatable checks: capture the existing message rather than recreating risk, compare scope, and check recent changes and service health. Record each result with a timestamp, including failed checks. If an approved fix exists, follow the knowledge-base procedure and note its version. Escalate changes beyond your authorization or skill level.

Escalation is not “forward and forget.” Give the next team impact, priority rationale, timeline, user contact, checks already performed and results, log locations, and the decision needed. Tell the user who owns the next step and when they will hear back. Urgent incidents may need an on-call channel as well as a ticket update. Put sensitive data only in authorized systems.

Test a permanent fix or workaround appropriately with the user and confirm service is restored for the expected task. Record a root cause only when supported by evidence; otherwise mark it unconfirmed. Include time, change, impact, and outcome. Send a closure summary and explain how to reopen the ticket. If resolution is not verified, keep it open according to policy and schedule the next update.
